title: Evaluating a Generate–Validate–Repair Pipeline for LLM‑based Network Configuration: a Paired, Emulation‑Grounded Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) to test whether integrating a deterministic network verifier into a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline reduces the rate of unsafe configuration applications from an LLM relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. Under the registered shared_initial_candidate semantics (one shared initial LLM generation per task, reused across arms), N = 240 paired intent→configuration tasks (144 in‑distribution, 48 distribution‑shift, 48 adversarial) were run with declared model gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5. All archived scoring artifacts record safe outcomes for every paired episode: baseline_success = 240/240; guarded_success = 240/240. The paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Because shared_initial_candidate semantics produced identical shared candidates that passed deterministic validation in every task, no validator‑triggered repairs occurred and the paired contrast is degenerate. We report the preregistered design, artifact‑grounded execution accounting, exact numerical outcomes, an artifact‑grounded failure analysis explaining the null paired result, and concrete recommendations for future informative GVR evaluations.

sections.introduction:
Translating high‑level operator intent into safe low‑level device configurations is a core NetOps challenge. Large language models (LLMs) can propose multi‑step configuration workflows but may err on ordering, dependencies, and invariants that matter at application time. Emulation‑grounded, closed‑loop evaluation—applying generated configs to emulated devices and deterministically checking semantic invariants—reveals operational failure modes not visible to text‑only metrics [1].

A common safety architecture is generate–validate–repair (GVR): an LLM proposes a candidate, a deterministic verifier checks semantic constraints, and a repair routine iteratively edits candidates when violations occur [2,3]. Prior work documents promise for GVR patterns but leaves open how much deterministic verification reduces unsafe applies under distribution shift or adversarial prompts, and how experimental design choices (notably paired semantics) affect detectability of verifier benefit [1–4].

We preregistered and executed a tightly specified paired experiment to estimate the paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded minus baseline) under shared_initial_candidate semantics. This manuscript (1) maps the preregistered estimand to archived analysis outputs and exact numeric results; (2) explains the degenerate paired outcome using archived execution accounting; and (3) gives artifact‑grounded recommendations for future, informative GVR evaluations.
sections.related_work:
Executable, emulation‑grounded benchmarks for LLM agents (e.g., NetConfArena) show that failures extend beyond syntax to planning and execution errors, motivating closed‑loop verification [1]. Work on automatic configuration repair and program repair documents generate–validate patterns and shows that validators can enable high repair coverage for many benchmarked faults, subject to verifier design and fault taxonomy [2,4]. Surveys and position papers synthesize agentic NetOps architectures, tool augmentation, and assurance contracts as crucial for operational safety [3,5]. Batfish and related configuration‑analysis engineering offer practical precedents for verifier design and incremental verification [6].

Our study differs by (a) a preregistered paired estimand; (b) explicit shared_initial_candidate execution semantics; (c) emulation‑grounded deterministic scoring; and (d) full archival of per‑call traces and validator traces to permit deterministic reconciliation of reported numbers to the archive.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: We preregistered study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01. Primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline, i.e., absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded − baseline) where unsafe_apply = 1 when a final configuration would cause a semantic safety violation when applied in the emulator and safe_apply = 0 otherwise. Bootstrap parameters (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) and the exact paired analysis procedure were preregistered.

Design and sampling: Paired design with shared_initial_candidate semantics: the adapter produced exactly one initial LLM generation per task and both arms reused that same generation. N = 240 distinct intent→configuration tasks were blocked into topology/vendor clusters and composed as: in‑distribution 60% (144), distribution‑shift 20% (48), adversarial‑prompt 20% (48). The declared model was gpt‑5‑mini and the deterministic verifier was deterministic_netops_validator_v5. The guarded pipeline could request up to one validator‑triggered repair per task under the preregistered adapter contract.

Scoring and exclusions: The verifier produces a binary final outcome (safe/unsafe) after applying the candidate to the emulator and checking semantic invariants. Preregistered exclusions included 'possible false‑safe' items (validator PASS but emulator unsafe outcome) and infra failures after allowed retries; sensitivity analyses for these cases were predefined. The retry policy permitted up to two infra retries. All counting and exclusion decisions used archived reconciliation artifacts and are reported exactly.
sections.results:
Execution accounting: The run completed per the preregistered plan: planned episodes = 480, completed episodes = 480, complete pairs = 240. Provider call accounting shows exactly one shared initial generation per task; total hosted model calls used = 240.

Primary outcomes: Every paired episode was scored safe under both arms. Baseline_safe = 240/240; Guarded_safe = 240/240. The paired contingency is n11 (both safe) = 240; n10 = n01 = n00 = 0. The paired estimator (guarded_unsafe_rate − baseline_unsafe_rate) = 0.00. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0.

Validator and repair activity: No validator‑triggered repairs were applied (repair_attempts = 0 across the run); every shared initial candidate passed deterministic validation. Difficulty composition observed across the task corpus: 192 tasks labeled "very_hard" (80.0%) and 48 tasks labeled "extreme" (20.0%).

Planned sensitivity channels (possible false‑safe, infra failures) were unused because no such flags or failures occurred; subgroup paired contrasts (in‑distribution, shift, adversarial) are degenerate given the all‑safe outcomes.
sections.discussion:
Artifact‑grounded explanation of the null paired contrast: Under preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics a single shared generation per task is reused across arms; the guarded arm can create paired discordance only by (a) the shared candidate failing validation and a repair being applied, or (b) the verifier flagging the candidate differently across arms. In this run every shared candidate passed deterministic validation and no repairs were invoked; thus the guarded arm could not alter final outcomes, producing the degenerate contingency and the observed 0.00 difference.

Design implications: The shared_initial_candidate contract reduces model‑call cost and yields a straightforward paired sample, but it makes the detectability of verifier benefit contingent on generator failures. To measure verifier causal effect in future studies, experimenters should: (A) allow independent initial generations per arm or randomized second draws in one arm; (B) increase adversary strength or variability to create validation failures; or (C) expand repair iteration budgets so repair behavior is exercised when validation fails. These recommendations follow directly from the archived provider and validator accounting that recorded one shared generation per task and zero repair usage.

Threats to validity and scope: Construct validity depends on verifier coverage: deterministic check sets can miss semantic fault classes. External validity is limited: tasks used a NetConfArena‑style synthetic emulation corpus; production multi‑vendor generalization is not established. Conclusion validity: realized baseline unsafe rate = 0 prevents inference about verifier benefit in this particular paired design; future power planning must target nonzero discordant pair expectations under the chosen generation semantics.
sections.conclusion:
We executed a fully preregistered, paired, emulation‑grounded evaluation of a GVR pipeline for LLM‑based network configuration. Observed outcome: all 240 paired tasks were safe under both baseline and guarded arms, yielding a paired difference = 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.00]; McNemar p = 1.0). This null paired result is explained mechanistically by the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics and the fact that every shared candidate passed the deterministic verifier, so the guarded arm had no opportunity to invoke repair. The archived execution and analysis artifacts support these exact numeric statements and provide a concrete guide for future GVR evaluations that intend to measure verifier causal effects: relax shared_initial_candidate constraints, increase adversary/perturbation strength, or enlarge repair budgets and instrumentation.

disclosure_statement: Execution used declared model gpt‑5‑mini via the registered adapter family hosted_netops_gvr_v1; the guarded pipeline used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and permitted up to one validator‑triggered repair per task. The study was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01; preregistration SHA‑256: 3e73ca0dc935a8754bf2dfbe6869ff989c47f1db0d93e2ca34809be8ebf95e26). The initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Human involvement: prior to the autonomy lock the human Research Director selected the topic family and constrained the initial master prompt; all literature search, preregistration, experiment selection, execution, analysis, and manuscript drafting were performed autonomously after the lock. The registered adapter used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one shared initial generation per task reused across both arms); therefore, within this run the guarded contrast could only differ from baseline if the shared initial candidate failed deterministic validation or a validator‑triggered repair were applied. A high‑level archived execution manifest and analysis bundle support the numeric results reported in this paper; detailed per‑file provenance is available in the archived bundle and is not reprinted here.
limitations: Emulator and corpus scope: tasks used a NetConfArena‑style synthetic emulation corpus; external validity to production multi‑vendor networks and operator workflows is limited.
Single model: a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) was tested; results do not generalize across models, prompts, or prompting strategies.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired design used one shared initial generation per task; this prevents generator variability between arms and makes observed verifier benefit contingent on initial candidate failures.
Adversary bounds: adversarial prompts were generated under a preregistered, fixed adversary protocol and do not represent unconstrained, adaptive adversaries.

Verifier coverage: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implements a finite check set; uncovered semantic fault classes may remain undetected, and planned false‑safe sensitivity channels were unused because no flags occurred in this run.
